\chapter{A Tree, Part by Part}
\label{ch:ml-a-tree-part-by-part}
\hlchaptermodality{54}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a tree and four of its parts in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C54-seed and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[maraṁ]{\ml{മരം} (maraṁ) — a tree}

\label{lesson:ML-C54-tree}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{nakṣatraṁ} mean, and what did \emph{veyil} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മരം}}
\textbf{\ml{മരം}} (\emph{maraṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{maram}, Kannada \emph{mara} and Telugu \emph{mrānu}. Four languages, one word, and no borrowing anywhere in it — this is a word the family had before it split.

It carries the standing tree and the cut timber on one shape. A carpenter's \ml{മരം} and a forest's \ml{മരം} are the same word, and Malayalam leaves it to the situation to say which is meant. English needs \emph{tree} and \emph{wood} to do that work.

Kerala's own tree, the coconut, gets a compound built on this one, and the ordinary word for a tree-climber is built on it too.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The thing the rest of this run takes apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maraṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{veyil}, then \emph{maraṁ}, and say which of the two the other one stands in
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മരം} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kompŭ]{\ml{കൊമ്പ്} (kompŭ) — a branch}

\label{lesson:ML-C54-branch}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maraṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കൊമ്പ്}}
\textbf{\ml{കൊമ്പ്}} (\emph{kompŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{kompu}. Malayalam puts one shape on anything that juts out and comes to a point: the branch of a tree, the horn of an ox, the tusk of an elephant, and the curved brass horn played at a temple festival.

That is a picture doing the work rather than a rule. Once you have seen the branch and the horn as one thing, the elephant's tusk needs no separate word, and Malayalam never gave it one.

The elephant sense is the one you are most likely to hear in Kerala, where the animal is a fixture of festival and of conversation both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the tree, and the part that reaches out from it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kompŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maraṁ}, then \emph{kompŭ}, and name two other things the second word covers
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കൊമ്പ്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[taṭi]{\ml{തടി} (taṭi) — a trunk, timber}

\label{lesson:ML-C54-trunk}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kompŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{തടി}}
\textbf{\ml{തടി}} (\emph{taṭi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a trunk, timber\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and it does three jobs on one shape: the trunk of a standing tree, the sawn timber that comes out of it, and — of a person — bulk or build.

The third sense is ordinary Malayalam and not unkind. To say somebody has \ml{തടി} is to say they are solidly made, and Kerala says it about a person the way English might say \emph{sturdy}.

Beside it sits \ml{തടിയൻ} (\emph{taṭiyan}), a heavy-set man, carrying that same he-word tail you met on the sun and the moon.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and this one describes people as well as trees.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{taṭi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kompŭ}, then \emph{taṭi}, and say which of the two you could saw
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{തടി} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a trunk, timber\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vērŭ]{\ml{വേര്} (vērŭ) — a root}

\label{lesson:ML-C54-root}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{taṭi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വേര്}}
\textbf{\ml{വേര്}} (\emph{vērŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{vēr} closely. The little ŭ at the end is the enunciative vowel you have been hearing since the salt-word and the lamp-word: a half-sounded release that Malayalam puts after a bare consonant and Tamil mostly does not write.

\ml{വേര്} reaches past the plant, as the English word does. The \ml{വേര്} of a matter is where it started, and a question about the \ml{വേര്} of a quarrel is a question about its cause.

The two languages arriving at the same figure from the same word is not a coincidence here — it is what roots look like to anybody who has pulled one up.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four: the tree, the branch, the trunk, and what holds it down.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vērŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{taṭi}, then \emph{vērŭ}, and say which end of the tree each one names
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വേര്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vittŭ]{\ml{വിത്ത്} (vittŭ) — a seed}

\label{lesson:ML-C54-seed}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vērŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വിത്ത്}}
\textbf{\ml{വിത്ത്}} (\emph{vittŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{vittu}, and it closes the tree by going back to where the tree started.

Like \ml{വേര്} it travels into the abstract. The \ml{വിത്ത്} of a plan is its beginning, and Malayalam will talk about sowing one. The doubled \emph{tt} in the middle is worth catching by ear — Malayalam holds it long, and the length is what separates this word from others in its neighbourhood.

Sowing season in Kerala is set by the rains rather than by a date, which is why the farming words in this language lean on the weather more than on the calendar.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run closes where a tree starts: a tree, a branch, the trunk, a root, a seed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vittŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{maraṁ}, \emph{kompŭ}, \emph{taṭi}, \emph{vērŭ}, \emph{vittŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വിത്ത്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
